feedback: Written before this candidate has raced; no outcome is claimed for it. Evidence: iteration 0 (baseline, body 0.16 m) is the best design at 356.6. It finishes the oval 20/20 at 1.65 s with oscillation 0.15, but its s-bend (0.17) and slalom (0.12) fail at max_error about 0.061 m. Iterations 3 to 6 show the baseline is a sharp local optimum: sensor y at 0.07 or 0.03, footprint 8 mm, and footprint 16 mm each cost the oval, and iteration 6 scored 78.8 with the oval at 0/20. Iterations 1 and 2 show that the wider array gives a partial bend gain (s-bend 0.17 to 0.24, slalom 0.12 to 0.19), but the oval loss was confounded with the lighter mass and narrower track. I kept the controller at baseline so the body length is the only variable. Next race: if the oval stays at 20/20 near 1.65 s with oscillation at or below 0.15 and bend progress rises slightly above 0.17 and 0.12, keep body_length 0.12 m and test a modest spread change (x plus or minus 0.028 m). If the oval drops or oscillation rises above about 0.2, return to body_length 0.16 m, since yaw inertia is damping the controller. If the bends do not move with the oval held, the bend limit is controller-side and geometry cannot fix it alone.
requested_changes: If the oval holds at 20/20 near 1.65 s and s-bend or slalom progress rises above 0.17 or 0.12, keep body_length 0.12 m and widen sensor x to plus or minus 0.028 m at 14 mm pitch, with mass 0.6 kg. Iterations 1 and 2 gave a partial bend gain from the wider array.

If the oval falls below 20/20 or steering_oscillation rises above about 0.2 (baseline 0.15), return body_length to 0.16 m, because iteration 0 is the reference and the controller appears tuned to the baseline yaw inertia.
Keep sensor y at 0.05 m, sensor_size at 0.012 m and mass at 0.6 kg for the next test. Iterations 3 to 6 show the oval collapses when any of these moves alone.
